snapshots.name: Croesus
snapshots.body: King of Lydia, the first barbarian Herodotus knows of to subdue Greeks. He asks Solon who is the happiest of men, loses his son, attacks Persia on a misread oracle, loses his kingdom, and ends as Cyrus’s adviser.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Candaules
snapshots.body: The last Heraclid king of Sardis, so convinced of his wife’s beauty that he made his bodyguard look at her naked — and was killed for it. The Greeks call him Myrsilus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Gyges
snapshots.body: Candaules’s favourite spearman, forced by the queen to choose between dying and killing his king. He took the kingdom, and the Delphic oracle confirmed it — adding that the Heraclids would be avenged in the fifth generation.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ardys
snapshots.body: Gyges’s son and successor, who took Priene and attacked Miletus, and in whose reign the Cimmerians took Sardis.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Sadyattes
snapshots.body: Ardys’s son, who began the long war against Miletus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Alyattes
snapshots.body: Croesus’s father, who inherited the Milesian war, burnt the temple of Athena of Assesos by accident, fell ill, and made peace on the oracle’s terms.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Atys
snapshots.body: Croesus’s able son, whom Croesus dreamed would die by an iron point — and who died on a boar hunt, by the spear of the guest he had been given as a guard.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Atys
snapshots.body: The ancient king from whose son Lydus the Lydian people took their name — a different man from Croesus’s son, five hundred years earlier.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pantaleon
snapshots.body: Croesus’s half-brother by a different mother, whom one faction tried to make king; Croesus had the man who tried it dragged over a carding-comb.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Heraclids
snapshots.body: The line descended from Heracles that ruled Sardis for twenty-two generations before Gyges.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Mermnadae
snapshots.body: The family of Gyges and Croesus, which took the Lydian throne from the Heraclids.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Alcaeus
snapshots.body: Son of Heracles, and the ancestor the Heraclid kings of Sardis traced themselves to.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Agron
snapshots.body: Son of Ninus, the first of the Heraclids to become king of Sardis.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ninus
snapshots.body: Agron’s father, in the Heraclid genealogy.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Belus
snapshots.body: Ninus’s father in the same genealogy; the older translation spells him Belos.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Myrsus
snapshots.body: Candaules’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Lydus
snapshots.body: Son of Atys, from whom the Lydians took their name; they had been called Meonians.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Adrastus
snapshots.body: A Phrygian prince who had killed his own brother by accident, was purified by Croesus, was given charge of Croesus’s son, killed him by accident too, and cut his own throat on the grave.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hyroeades
snapshots.body: The Mardian soldier who watched a Lydian climb down the unguarded cliff after a fallen helmet, and so found the way into Sardis.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pactyas
snapshots.body: The Lydian left in charge of Croesus’s gold, who used it to raise a revolt against Cyrus and then fled from city to city until the Chians sold him for a stretch of land.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cyrus
snapshots.body: Cyrus the Great: the grandson Astyages tried to have killed, raised by a herdsman, who overthrew the Medes, took Sardis and Babylon, and died fighting Tomyris beyond the Araxes.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Astyages
snapshots.body: The last king of the Medes, who dreamed twice about his daughter, ordered his grandson killed, served Harpagos his own son at dinner, and lost his kingdom to the grandson who survived.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Harpagos
snapshots.body: Astyages’s kinsman, ordered to expose the infant Cyrus and unable to do it. Astyages fed him his own son for it; Harpagos waited years and then handed Astyages’s army to Cyrus. He afterwards conquered Ionia for Persia. The two editions spell him Harpagos and Harpagus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Deioces
snapshots.body: The Mede who made himself indispensable as a judge, was elected king, built Agbatana with its seven coloured walls, and made himself invisible to his subjects on purpose.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Phraortes
snapshots.body: Deioces’s son, who subdued the Persians and died attacking the Assyrians of Nineveh.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cyaxares
snapshots.body: Phraortes’s son, who first organised the Median army into companies, besieged Nineveh, and was interrupted by the Scythians for twenty-eight years.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mandane
snapshots.body: Astyages’s daughter and Cyrus’s mother, married off to a quiet Persian because of what her father dreamed about her.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cambyses
snapshots.body: Cyrus’s father — a Persian of good family whom Astyages judged harmless. Not the Cambyses who succeeds Cyrus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cambyses
snapshots.body: Cyrus’s son, to whom Cyrus handed Croesus and the kingdom before riding against the Massagetai. Book 3 is largely his.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mitradates
snapshots.body: The herdsman ordered to expose the infant Cyrus, whose own newborn son had just died; his wife asked for the living child instead.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Kyno
snapshots.body: The herdsman’s wife, called Spako in Median and Kyno in Greek — both meaning "dog", which is how the story of the infant Cyrus being suckled by a bitch got started.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Artembares
snapshots.body: The Mede whose son was whipped by the boy Cyrus playing at being king — the complaint that made Astyages look at the boy’s face.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mazares
snapshots.body: The Mede sent to put down Pactyas and reduce the Ionians; he died in the middle of it.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Tabalos
snapshots.body: The Persian left as governor of Sardis, besieged in the acropolis by Pactyas.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Darius
snapshots.body: Darius son of Hystaspes, later king of Persia, who appears in Book 1 only as the young man in Cyrus’s dream and as the future plunderer of a Babylonian statue. The two editions spell him Darius and Dareios.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hystaspes
snapshots.body: Darius’s father, a Persian in Cyrus’s army whom Cyrus sent home to watch his son after the dream.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Tomyris
snapshots.body: Queen of the Massagetai, who refused Cyrus’s offer of marriage, warned him to keep to his own country, lost her son to his trick with the wine, and put his head in a skin of blood so that he could drink his fill.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Spargapises
snapshots.body: Tomyris’s son, taken by Cyrus’s stratagem with the feast and the unmixed wine, who asked to be unbound and killed himself.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Labynetus
snapshots.body: The king of Babylon, named twice — as one of the two mediators of the peace between Lydia and Media, and as the ruler Cyrus’s canals were dug against.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Syennesis
snapshots.body: The Cilician, who with Labynetus mediated the peace between Alyattes and Cyaxares.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Magians
snapshots.body: One of the Median tribes, and the caste that reads dreams and portents and performs the Persian sacrifices; their reading of Astyages’s dream is what sets the whole story going.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Chaldeans
snapshots.body: The priests of Bel at Babylon, who told Herodotus what stood in the temple and what had been taken from it.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Solon
snapshots.body: The Athenian lawgiver, who left Athens for ten years so that his laws could not be unmade, came to Sardis, and refused to call Croesus happy while he was still alive.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Tellus
snapshots.body: The Athenian Solon names as the happiest of men: he lived well, saw his children’s children, and died fighting at Eleusis and was buried where he fell.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cleobis
snapshots.body: One of two Argive brothers who pulled their mother’s ox-cart to the temple of Hera; she prayed for the best thing a man can have, and they died in their sleep.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Biton
snapshots.body: Cleobis’s brother, named with him as second happiest.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Peisistratus
snapshots.body: Tyrant of Athens three times over: once by wounding himself and getting a bodyguard, once with a tall woman dressed as Athena riding into the city beside him, and once by force and mercenaries.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Megacles
snapshots.body: Son of Alcmaeon and leader of the faction of the shore, who brought Peisistratus back to Athens by marrying him to his daughter, and drove him out again when the marriage displeased him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Lycurgus
snapshots.body: Son of Aristolaides and leader of the faction of the plain — the Athenian rival of Megacles and Peisistratus, not the Spartan lawgiver of the next few pages.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Alcmaeon
snapshots.body: Megacles’s father, named in the Athenian faction fighting.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hippocrates
snapshots.body: Peisistratus’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Lygdamis
snapshots.body: The Naxian who gave Peisistratus money and men for his third return, and was set up as tyrant of Naxos for it.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Lycurgus
snapshots.body: The lawgiver who gave Sparta its whole constitution — brought from Crete, or given by the Pythia, depending on who is telling it — and turned the worst-governed Greeks into the best.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Leon
snapshots.body: A king of Sparta in the generation before Anaxandrides, under whom the Spartans beat everyone except Tegea.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hegesicles
snapshots.body: Leon’s fellow-king at Sparta.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Anaxandrides
snapshots.body: King of Sparta at the time of Croesus’s embassy.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ariston
snapshots.body: Anaxandrides’s fellow-king at Sparta when Croesus sent for an alliance.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ariston
snapshots.body: Childless by two wives, he took a third by tricking his closest friend out of her with a sworn exchange of gifts. When the servant announced the birth he counted the months on his fingers and denied the child on oath — one sentence, thought nothing of at the time, that unseated Demaratus years later.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Lichas
snapshots.body: One of the Spartan "Well-doers", who found the bones of Orestes under a blacksmith’s forge at Tegea by taking the smith’s talk about a seven-foot coffin literally.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Orestes
snapshots.body: Son of Agamemnon, whose bones the oracle told Sparta to fetch home from Tegea before they could beat the Tegeans.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Agamemnon
snapshots.body: Orestes’s father, named in the oracle.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Othryades
snapshots.body: The one Spartan left standing after the Battle of the Champions at Thyrea, who stripped the Argive dead and stayed on the field — and afterwards killed himself for shame at outliving his three hundred.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Chilon
snapshots.body: The Spartan sage who warned Hippocrates, after the cauldron boiled over without a fire, not to have a son.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Periander
snapshots.body: Tyrant of Corinth, son of Cypselus, who tortured the crew that had thrown Arion overboard, and who took his lesson in government from Thrasybulus’s walk through a cornfield.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cypselus
snapshots.body: Periander’s father and tyrant of Corinth before him; the treasury at Delphi that bears the Corinthian name is really his.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Thrasybulus
snapshots.body: Tyrant of Miletus and Periander’s guest-friend, who got wind of Alyattes’s intentions and had the city’s last grain heaped in the marketplace for the herald to see.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Arion
snapshots.body: The lyre-player of Methymna, robbed by his own crew, who asked to sing once more in full costume, jumped overboard, and was carried to Taenarum on a dolphin’s back.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Thales
snapshots.body: Thales of Miletus, who foretold the year of the eclipse that stopped the battle between the Medes and the Lydians, and who is said to have diverted the Halys so Croesus could cross.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Bias
snapshots.body: Bias of Priene, who talked Croesus out of building a fleet by telling him the islanders were buying horses — and who advised the Ionians, too late, to sail away and found one city in Sardinia.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pittacus
snapshots.body: Pittacus of Mytilene, named as the other candidate for the sage who gave Croesus the advice about the islanders and their horses.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aristodicos
snapshots.body: The man of Kyme who, told by the oracle to give up the suppliant Pactyas, walked round the temple pulling nests down from the eaves until the god objected — and then asked the god the obvious question.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Arganthonios
snapshots.body: King of Tartessos, who reigned eighty years and lived a hundred and twenty, and offered the Phocaeans his whole country to settle in.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Amasis
snapshots.body: King of Egypt, named in Book 1 as one of Croesus’s allies and as the man Solon visited.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Minos
snapshots.body: Son of Europa, who ruled the sea in the old time and whose subjects the Carians were before they came to the mainland.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Sarpedon
snapshots.body: Minos’s brother, driven out of Crete, who led the Termilai into the land that became Lycia.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Lycos
snapshots.body: Son of Pandion, exiled from Athens by his brother Aegeus, from whom the Lycians took their name.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pandion
snapshots.body: Lycos’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Europa
snapshots.body: The king’s daughter carried off from Tyre — the second of the four abductions with which Herodotus opens the quarrel between Europe and Asia.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Io
snapshots.body: Daughter of Inachus, carried off from Argos by Phoenician traders — the first abduction, and the beginning of the whole business.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Inachus
snapshots.body: Io’s father, king of Argos.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Medea
snapshots.body: The king of Colchis’s daughter, carried off by Greeks in a warship up the Phasis — the third abduction.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Helen
snapshots.body: Carried off by Alexander, which the Persians say was the fourth abduction and the one the Greeks made a war of, for a single woman.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Alexander
snapshots.body: The son of Priam — Paris — who carried off Helen because earlier abductions had gone unpunished. Not the Alexander who rules Macedon later in the Histories.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Priam
snapshots.body: Alexander’s father, king of Troy.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Midas
snapshots.body: King of Phrygia, son of Gordias, the only barbarian before Gyges to dedicate offerings at Delphi — his throne.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Gordias
snapshots.body: Midas’s father, and also the father of the Adrastus who killed Croesus’s son.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Amphiaraus
snapshots.body: The seer whose oracle Croesus tested along with the others, and to whose shrine he sent a shield and spear of solid gold. The two editions spell him Amphiaraus and Amphiaraos.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Zeus
snapshots.body: Invoked in Book 1 as the Purifier, the Protector of Suppliants and the Guardian of Friendship, all three by Adrastus over the body of Croesus’s son.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Apollo
snapshots.body: The god of Delphi, called Loxias where he speaks in oracles and Ismenian where Croesus sends him a tripod at Thebes. He gave Croesus three years’ grace and could not do more.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Pythian prophetess
snapshots.body: The priestess through whom Apollo answers at Delphi — who told Gyges the Heraclids would be avenged, told Croesus he would destroy a great empire, and told Sparta to fetch the bones of Orestes.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Athena
snapshots.body: Athena of Assesos, whose temple Alyattes burnt by accident and had to rebuild twice before he could be cured.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hera
snapshots.body: At whose Argive festival Cleobis and Biton pulled the cart, and whose priestess prayed for the best thing a man can have.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aphrodite
snapshots.body: Worshipped as Aphrodite Urania, whose temple at Ascalon the Scythians plundered and were punished with a lasting disease; the Assyrians call her Mylitta.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Heracles
snapshots.body: Ancestor, through Alcaeus, of the old kings of Sardis.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Persians
snapshots.body: Herodotus’s subject: the people whose learned men give him his opening account of the quarrel, and who under Cyrus go from subjects of the Medes to masters of Asia.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Lydians
snapshots.body: Croesus’s people, the first to strike coin and to keep retail shops, and the first barbarians the Greeks paid tribute to.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Medes
snapshots.body: The empire Cyrus overthrew, first to revolt from Assyria and first to be organised into a kingdom.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Ionians
snapshots.body: The twelve cities on the Asian coast that Croesus subdued and Cyrus took, and whose refusal to help Cyrus first cost them their liberty.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Aeolians
snapshots.body: The Greeks of the coast north of Ionia, subdued with them. The two editions spell them Aeolians and Aiolians.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Dorians
snapshots.body: The third of the three Greek divisions, of whom the five cities of the Triopian temple are the Asian branch.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Hellenes
snapshots.body: Herodotus’s word for the Greeks as one people, set against the barbarians from the first sentence of the work.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Athenians
snapshots.body: Of Pelasgian stock and never moved from their land; under Peisistratus in Croesus’s day, and the people Croesus judged the first among the Ionians.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Lacedaemonians
snapshots.body: The Spartans, whom Croesus chose as allies because they were the first of the Dorians — worst-governed of the Greeks once, and best-governed since Lycurgus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Scythians
snapshots.body: The nomads who drove the Cimmerians out of their homes, followed them into Asia, and held the upper country for twenty-eight years before the Medes got them drunk and killed them.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Cimmerians
snapshots.body: Driven from their own land by the Scythians, they took Sardis in the reign of Ardys — all of it but the citadel.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Massagetai
snapshots.body: Tomyris’s people, beyond the Araxes: a great and warlike nation who share their wives, eat their old, and killed Cyrus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Babylonians
snapshots.body: The people of the greatest city Herodotus knows, taken by Cyrus when he drew off the Euphrates and walked in along the riverbed while they were at a festival.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Assyrians
snapshots.body: Rulers of Upper Asia for five hundred and twenty years before the Medes revolted.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Phoenicians
snapshots.body: The traders who, in the Persian account, began the whole quarrel by carrying off Io from Argos.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Egyptians
snapshots.body: Croesus’s allies through Amasis, and a people Herodotus will spend his entire second book on.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Milesians
snapshots.body: Of Miletus: at war with Lydia for eleven years, then the only Ionians to make terms with Cyrus on the old footing.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Samians
snapshots.body: Who seized the great bronze bowl the Lacedaemonians were sending to Croesus — or bought it from the men who did, depending on which side is telling it.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Chians
snapshots.body: Who alone helped the Milesians in the Lydian war, and who afterwards dragged Pactyas out of the temple of Athena and handed him over for a piece of land.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Phocaeans
snapshots.body: The first Greeks to make long sea voyages, who sailed away from Ionia rather than submit, sank half their own fleet’s worth of enemies off Corsica, and dropped an iron bar in the sea to swear by. The two editions spell them Phocaeans and Phocaians.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Carians
snapshots.body: Once islanders and subjects of Minos, called Leleges then; they claim to be native to the mainland, and gave the Greeks the crest, the shield-grip and the blazon.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Caunians
snapshots.body: Neighbours of the Carians who say they came from Crete, and who once drove out foreign gods by beating the air with their spears as far as the border.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Lycians
snapshots.body: Sarpedon’s people, the Termilai renamed after Lycos; they reckon descent by the mother, and burnt their own women and treasure before dying on Harpagos’s swords. The two editions spell them Lycians and Lykians.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Pedasians
snapshots.body: The only people of the Halicarnassus region who gave Harpagos trouble; their priestess of Athena grows a beard when disaster is coming.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Pelasgians
snapshots.body: The people the Greeks were before they were Greeks — whose language Herodotus cannot determine except by what their descendants still speak.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Argives
snapshots.body: Cleobis and Biton’s people, and the losers of the Battle of the Champions at Thyrea.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Corinthians
snapshots.body: In whose treasury at Delphi Gyges’s gold stands — though it belongs properly to Cypselus — and who tell the story of Arion.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Lesbians
snapshots.body: Who agree with the Corinthians about Arion and the dolphin.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Tegeans
snapshots.body: The Arcadians who beat Sparta and made the prisoners work their own fields in the fetters they had brought, until the bones of Orestes changed the war.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Arcadians
snapshots.body: Acorn-eaters, whose land the Spartans asked the oracle for and did not get.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Delphians
snapshots.body: Keepers of the oracle, who tell Herodotus which offerings are whose and gave the Lydians precedence in consulting the god.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Cretans
snapshots.body: Whom Herodotus supposes to have been the crew that carried off Europa.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Phrygians
snapshots.body: Adrastus’s people, and one of the nations inside the Halys that Croesus ruled.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Mysians
snapshots.body: Of Mysian Olympus, whose boar ruined the fields and cost Croesus his son.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Paphlagonians
snapshots.body: One of the peoples inside the Halys ruled by Croesus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Thracians
snapshots.body: The Thynian and Bithynian Thracians of Asia, among Croesus’s subjects.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Syrians
snapshots.body: The people on the Cappadocian side of the Halys, whom the Greeks call Cappadocians.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Armenians
snapshots.body: From whose mountains the Halys and the Tigris come down.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Matienians
snapshots.body: From whose mountains the Gyndes rises — the river Cyrus punished by splitting it into three hundred and sixty channels.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Arabians
snapshots.body: Who call Aphrodite Alilat, and from whom, with the Assyrians, the Persians learned to worship her.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Achaeans
snapshots.body: Who drove the Ionians out of the Peloponnese, and whose twelve districts the Ionians copied.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Tyrsenians
snapshots.body: The Etruscans, said by the Lydians to be their own emigrants, sent out under Tyrsenus when the famine had lasted eighteen years.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Carthaginians
snapshots.body: Who joined the Etruscans against the Phocaean settlers on Corsica.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Tartessians
snapshots.body: Arganthonios’s people, beyond the Pillars, with whom the Phocaeans became friends.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Ephesians
snapshots.body: The first Greeks Croesus attacked, who ran a rope from their walls to the temple of Artemis and dedicated the city to her.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Telmessians
snapshots.body: The interpreters of portents whom Croesus consulted about the snakes in the suburb of Sardis, and whose answer came too late.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Leleges
snapshots.body: The name the Carians went by while they were islanders and subjects of Minos.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Min
snapshots.body: The first man to be king of Egypt, who dammed the Nile away from Memphis and founded the city on the reclaimed ground. The older translation spells him Men.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Nitocris
snapshots.body: The one queen in the priests’ list of three hundred and thirty kings, who avenged her murdered brother by drowning his killers at a feast and then threw herself into a room full of ashes.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Moeris
snapshots.body: The king before whose reign the Nile needed only eight cubits to flood Egypt, and whose name the great lake carries. The two editions spell the lake Moeris and Moiris.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Sesostris
snapshots.body: The conqueror who set out with a fleet from the Arabian gulf, marched through Asia into Europe, and left carved pillars behind him — with a woman’s parts cut on them where the people gave in without a fight.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pheros
snapshots.body: Sesostris’s son, blinded for throwing a spear into the flooding Nile, and cured after ten years by a remedy that cost the lives of a great many women.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Proteus
snapshots.body: The king of Memphis who held Helen and the stolen treasure in Egypt for the whole length of the Trojan war, and sent Alexander away — the story Herodotus believes over Homer’s.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Thonis
snapshots.body: The warden of the Canobic mouth who arrested Alexander’s servants and reported him to Proteus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Rhampsinitos
snapshots.body: The rich king whose treasury a mason’s two sons robbed through a movable stone — the best story in Book 2 — and who ended by marrying his daughter to the thief.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cheops
snapshots.body: The king who shut the temples, set the whole people to work on his pyramid for twenty years, and sold his own daughter’s favours to pay for it.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Chephren
snapshots.body: Cheops’s brother and successor, who ruled in the same manner for fifty-six years; the Egyptians will not willingly say either brother’s name.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mykerinos
snapshots.body: Cheops’s son, who opened the temples again and gave the people back their lives — and was told by the oracle that he had six years to live because Egypt was meant to suffer a hundred and fifty. He answered by lighting lamps and living the nights as well.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Asychis
snapshots.body: The king who made a law that a man might borrow on his father’s corpse, and built a pyramid of brick with an inscription telling it not to compare itself with the stone ones.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Anysis
snapshots.body: The blind king of the city of the same name, who fled into the marshes when the Ethiopians came and hid there fifty years on a floating island of ash and earth.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Sabacos
snapshots.body: The Ethiopian who ruled Egypt for fifty years without putting anyone to death, and left because of a dream rather than wait for it to come true.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Sethos
snapshots.body: The priest of Hephaistos who despised the warrior class and was saved from Sennacherib by field-mice that ate the Assyrians’ bowstrings overnight.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Psammetichos
snapshots.body: One of the twelve kings, driven out and returned with the bronze men the oracle promised; he reunited Egypt, opened it to Greek traders, and shut two children away with a mute shepherd to find out which language came first. The two editions spell him Psammetichos and Psammetichus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Necos
snapshots.body: Psammetichos’s son, who began the canal to the Red Sea, gave it up when the oracle warned him, and sent Phoenicians to sail round Libya. The older translation spells him Necos; he is also the father Sabacos killed.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Psammis
snapshots.body: Necos’s son, who reigned six years, invaded Ethiopia, and gave the Eleians the obvious answer about their own games.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Apries
snapshots.body: Psammis’s son, the most prosperous king but one until his army went over to Amasis; he was kept alive in his own palace and then handed to the Egyptians, who strangled him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Patarbemis
snapshots.body: The man of reputation Apries sent to fetch Amasis back, and whose ears and nose Apries cut off when he came back without him — which lost Apries the rest of his subjects.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ladice
snapshots.body: The Cyrenaean woman Amasis married, who prayed to Aphrodite when he could not come to her and afterwards sent the goddess a statue.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Amyrtaios
snapshots.body: The only man in seven hundred years to find the floating island in the marshes where Anysis had hidden.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Rhodopis
snapshots.body: The Thracian courtesan the Greeks credit with the third pyramid — wrongly, Herodotus says, since she lived generations later. She spent a tenth of her fortune on iron roasting-spits at Delphi.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Iadmon
snapshots.body: The Samian who owned Rhodopis, and Aesop before her.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aesop
snapshots.body: The fable-maker, named here as Rhodopis’s fellow-slave, for whose killing the Delphians had to pay compensation.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Charaxos
snapshots.body: The man of Mytilene who bought Rhodopis’s freedom at great expense, and was mocked for it in his sister’s poetry.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Sappho
snapshots.body: Charaxos’s sister, named as the lyric poet who made a song about what her brother had spent his money on.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Etearchus
snapshots.body: King of the Ammonians, who told the Nasamonians’ story of the five young men who crossed the desert and came to a city of small black men beside a river full of crocodiles.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Archander
snapshots.body: Son-in-law of Danaus, after whom a city in the Delta is named; Herodotus doubts the name is Egyptian at all.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hecataeus
snapshots.body: The historian who traced his own descent to a god in the sixteenth generation, and was shown three hundred and forty-five wooden statues at Thebes to correct him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Menelaus
snapshots.body: Helen’s husband, who came to Egypt for her after Troy fell, got her back from Proteus, and repaid the Egyptians by sacrificing two of their children for a wind.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hector
snapshots.body: Priam’s elder and abler son, whose existence Herodotus uses as the proof that Troy would have given Helen up if it had had her.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Homer
snapshots.body: Whom Herodotus supposes to have invented the river Ocean, to have known the Egyptian version of Helen and set it aside as less suitable for poetry, and to have lived four hundred years before his own day.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hesiod
snapshots.body: Named with Homer as the pair who made the Greeks their theogony, gave the gods their titles and described their forms.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Perseus
snapshots.body: Whose watchtower stands on the Egyptian coast and whose sandal turns up at Chemmis; the people there say he was theirs, being descended from Danaus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Danaus
snapshots.body: Of Chemmis, from whom the people there trace Perseus; his daughters brought the rite of the Thesmophoria out of Egypt. The two editions spell him Danaus and Danaos.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Lynceus
snapshots.body: Named with Danaus as a man of Chemmis who sailed to Greece.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Amphitryon
snapshots.body: Heracles’s mortal father — of Egyptian descent, the Egyptians say, which is why the Greeks are wrong about which Heracles is older.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Alcmene
snapshots.body: Heracles’s mother, named with Amphitryon in the same argument.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Melampus
snapshots.body: Son of Amytheon, who Herodotus thinks brought the rite of Dionysus into Greece from Egypt, having learned it from Cadmus and the Phoenicians.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Amytheon
snapshots.body: Melampus’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cadmus
snapshots.body: The Phoenician from whom Melampus is supposed to have learned the Egyptian rites. The two editions spell him Cadmus and Cadmos.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Semele
snapshots.body: Cadmus’s daughter, the mother of the Greek Dionysus — sixteen hundred years after the Egyptian one, on Herodotus’s reckoning.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Penelope
snapshots.body: Of whom the Greeks say Pan was born, and Hermes — eight hundred years after the Egyptian Pan.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Linus
snapshots.body: The song the Egyptians call Maneros, sung in Phoenicia and Cyprus under other names, and the one song the Egyptians have.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Danae
snapshots.body: Perseus’s mother, named in the Chemmite genealogy.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hephaestus
snapshots.body: The god the Greeks call Hephaestus and the Egyptians Ptah, whose priests at Memphis are Herodotus’s main informants; his temple is the one every king adds to. The two editions spell him Hephaestus and Hephaistos.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Isis
snapshots.body: Whose figure is a woman with cow’s horns, and who is Demeter in Greek. Cows are sacred to her and are never sacrificed.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Osiris
snapshots.body: Isis’s fellow — Dionysus in Greek — whose sufferings are represented at Saïs on the night the Egyptians call the Lamps.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Dionysus
snapshots.body: Osiris under his Greek name, whose rites Melampus is supposed to have brought to Greece, and who with Demeter rules the world below in the Egyptian account. The two editions spell him Dionysus and Dionysos.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Demeter
snapshots.body: Isis under her Greek name, ruler with Dionysus of the world below.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Leto
snapshots.body: Honoured at Buto, where the floating island is and where the oracle spoke; in the Egyptian story she was Apollo’s nurse, not his mother.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Artemis
snapshots.body: Honoured at Bubastis with the greatest festival in Egypt; in the Egyptian account she is the daughter of Dionysus and Isis.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ares
snapshots.body: Honoured at Papremis, where the festival is a real fight with clubs at the temple gate.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pan
snapshots.body: One of the eight oldest gods in the Egyptian reckoning, painted and carved with a goat’s face and a he-goat’s legs; the Mendesians will not sacrifice goats because of him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hermes
snapshots.body: Whose images the Greeks make as they do because they learned it from the Pelasgians, not from the Egyptians; and whom the Greeks call Pan’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Poseidon
snapshots.body: A god the Egyptians say they do not know, and who came to the Greeks from the Libyans.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Dioscuri
snapshots.body: Named with Poseidon among the gods the Egyptians say they have never heard of.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ammon
snapshots.body: The god of the oracle in the Libyan desert, whose name is the Egyptian name for Zeus; his image is a ram, and that is why the Thebans will not sacrifice sheep.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Helios
snapshots.body: The Sun, honoured at Heliopolis; the Egyptians say he once rose where he now sets, twice over, within written memory.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Typhon
snapshots.body: Set under his Greek name, whom Horus deposed to become the last divine king of Egypt.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Ethiopians
snapshots.body: Egypt’s neighbours up the Nile, whose king Sabacos held Egypt for fifty years, and among whom the Deserters settled beyond Meroe.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Libyans
snapshots.body: Whose land runs west from Egypt; the Marea and Apis people claimed to be Libyans and not Egyptians so as to eat cow’s flesh, and were told by the oracle that all the Nile waters is Egypt.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Colchians
snapshots.body: Whom Herodotus judges to be Egyptian by descent on three grounds — their skin, their hair, and the fact that they circumcise.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Nasamonians
snapshots.body: The Libyan people of the Syrtis whose five adventurous young men crossed the desert and found a city of small dark men by a great river running east; Book 4 calls them the Nasamones and describes their year — inland for the dates, the coast for the summer.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Ammonians
snapshots.body: Etearchus’s people, at the oracle of Ammon; colonists, Herodotus says, from both Egypt and Ethiopia.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Mendesians
snapshots.body: Who count Pan among the eight oldest gods, keep goats sacred, and have the story about the he-goat that is not to be repeated.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Samothracians
snapshots.body: Who perform the mysteries of the Cabeiri, learned from the Pelasgians who used to live on the island.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Eleians
snapshots.body: Who came to Psammis boasting that their arrangement of the Olympic games was the justest in the world, and were told to let strangers compete if they meant it.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Calasirians
snapshots.body: One of the two Egyptian warrior classes, with their own districts and their twelve aruras of tax-free land.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Hermotybians
snapshots.body: The other Egyptian warrior class, named with the Calasirians.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Celts
snapshots.body: Beyond the Pillars of Heracles, at whose country the Ister begins.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Trojans
snapshots.body: Who, Herodotus argues, would have given Helen back if they had had her, since they were losing their lives for her by the day.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Cilicians
snapshots.body: Named as the people whose land Cilicia is, in the argument about what makes a country.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Smerdis
snapshots.body: Cyrus’s younger son, whom Cambyses had Prexaspes kill in secret after dreaming that he would sit on the throne. Almost nobody in Persia knew he was dead, which is what made the impersonation possible.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Smerdis
snapshots.body: Cyrus’s younger son, killed in secret on Cambyses’s orders by Prexaspes — a death so few Persians knew of that a stranger could later take his name.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: The Magian
snapshots.body: The brother left in charge of Cambyses’s household, who seized the throne because he knew the real Smerdis was dead and that almost nobody else did. He was his namesake, and he reigned seven months and did his subjects good; the Persians killed him when Otanes found out, through his own daughter, that the man in the bed had no ears.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Magian
snapshots.body: The usurper who reigned as Smerdis for seven months, remitted military service and tribute for three years, and was mourned by every nation in Asia except the Persians.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: The Magian
snapshots.body: The usurper, killed in his own chamber by Darius and Gobryas wrestling in the dark — and commemorated afterwards by the Magophonia, the one day in the year a Magian may not walk out of doors.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: The two Magians
snapshots.body: The usurper and Patizeithes his brother, who between them held Persia for seven months: one on the throne, the other managing everything for him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Patizeithes
snapshots.body: The Magian left as caretaker of Cambyses’s household, who put his brother on the throne and ran the kingdom for him. He is named once.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Nitetis
snapshots.body: Apries’s daughter, whom Amasis sent to Cambyses in place of his own — and who told Cambyses whose daughter she really was. That, in the Egyptian telling, is why Persia invaded.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cassandane
snapshots.body: Cyrus’s wife and Cambyses’s mother, whom the Persian account says Cambyses avenged on Egypt because Cyrus had slighted her.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pharnaspes
snapshots.body: Cassandane’s father, and Otanes’s, of the Achaemenid family.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Phanes
snapshots.body: The Halicarnassian mercenary who quarrelled with Apries, fled to Cambyses, and told the Persians how to cross the waterless desert. The Greeks in Egyptian service cut his sons’ throats in front of him before the battle and drank the blood.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Psammenitos
snapshots.body: Amasis’s son, king of Egypt for six months, who did not weep to see his daughter carrying water or his son led out to die, and wept at the sight of an old drinking-companion begging. Cambyses spared him and then killed him for plotting.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Prexaspes
snapshots.body: Cambyses’s most trusted Persian, who killed Smerdis for him, told him the truth about what the Persians said of him, watched Cambyses shoot his own son through the heart to prove his hand was steady, and finally threw himself off a tower after telling Persia the truth.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Apis
snapshots.body: The sacred calf of Memphis, whom the Greeks call Epaphos: black with a white diamond, a double hair in its tail, the marks of an eagle and a beetle. Cambyses stabbed it in the thigh and it died in the temple, which the Egyptians say is why he went mad.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Ichthyophagoi
snapshots.body: The Fish-eaters of Elephantine, who knew the Ethiopian tongue and were sent ahead of Cambyses’s army as spies with gifts.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Achaimenes
snapshots.body: Darius’s son, killed with his army in Egypt by Inaros the Libyan — Herodotus looking forward out of his own narrative.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Inaros
snapshots.body: The Libyan who destroyed Achaimenes and his Persians in Egypt.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Polycrates
snapshots.body: Tyrant of Samos, who took the island with fifteen men, made himself the first Greek since Minos to aim at ruling the sea, and was crucified at Magnesia by a Persian governor he had never fought. Herodotus will not repeat what was done to his body.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aiakes
snapshots.body: Polycrates’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Syloson
snapshots.body: Polycrates’s brother, exiled — and the man who gave Darius a red cloak in Egypt for nothing, years before Darius was king, and afterwards asked for Samos and got it.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pantagnotos
snapshots.body: Polycrates’s other brother, killed when Polycrates took sole power.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Maiandrios
snapshots.body: Polycrates’s secretary, left in charge of Samos, who tried to hand the island over to a free constitution and was refused; he ended by opening the treasury to the Persians and escaping through a tunnel.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Charilaos
snapshots.body: Maiandrios’s half-mad brother, who was let out of the cells, saw the Persians sitting unarmed, took the mercenaries and killed them — and so brought the massacre of Samos on the island.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Archias
snapshots.body: One of the two Lacedaemonians who broke into Samos and died inside it; Herodotus met his grandson, also Archias, at Pitana.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Archias
snapshots.body: The grandson of the Archias who died at Samos, whom Herodotus met and who honoured the Samians above all strangers because they had buried his grandfather at public cost.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Lycopas
snapshots.body: The other Lacedaemonian who followed the routed Samians inside the walls and was cut off there with Archias.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Samios
snapshots.body: The son the first Archias named for Samos, and the father of the Archias Herodotus met.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eupalinos
snapshots.body: The Megarian engineer of the Samian tunnel, seven furlongs through a mountain and open at both ends — the first of the three greatest Greek works Herodotus knows.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Naustrophos
snapshots.body: Eupalinos’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Oroetes
snapshots.body: The Persian governor of Sardis who had Polycrates crucified out of nothing but pique at a slight he had imagined, and murdered Mitrobates and his son as well. Darius had him killed by a letter read out to his own guards.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mitrobates
snapshots.body: Governor of Daskyleion, who taunted Oroetes at the king’s door with not having taken Samos, and was killed for it with his son.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Bagaios
snapshots.body: The son of Artontes who drew the lot, went to Sardis with a bundle of letters, and had Oroetes’s own bodyguard kill him by reading the last one aloud.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Artontes
snapshots.body: Bagaios’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Melissa
snapshots.body: Periander’s wife, whom he killed, and whose ghost would not name the hiding-place of a deposit until he had burnt real clothes for her in the pit at Corinth.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Procles
snapshots.body: Despot of Epidauros and Melissa’s father, who asked his two grandsons whether they knew who had killed their mother — and ruined the younger one.
