snapshots.body: At the height of their wealth from gold and silver mines, who refused the exiled Samians a loan and lost a hundred talents and their fields for it — as their oracle about the white council-house had warned them.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Aeginetans
snapshots.body: Who with the Cretans defeated the Samian settlers at Kydonia and dedicated the ships’ boar-prows in the temple of Athena on Aegina.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Otanes
snapshots.body: Son of Pharnaspes, the first to suspect that the man on the throne was not Smerdis, and the one who proved it through his own daughter. He argued for democracy against the other six, withdrew from the contest for the throne on condition that his house be free, and it still was in Herodotus’s day.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Phaidyme
snapshots.body: Otanes’s daughter, married to the king; her father asked her to feel for the ears of the man asleep beside her, knowing Cyrus had cut the Magian’s off. She did it, and there were none.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Atossa
snapshots.body: Cyrus’s daughter, wife of her brother Cambyses, then of the Magian, then of Darius — and the woman who, prompted in bed by a Greek physician, set Darius on Greece.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Intaphrenes
snapshots.body: One of the seven, whom Otanes brought in; he later forced the palace gates believing the law let him, and Darius destroyed his whole family but for the brother and son his wife chose. The two editions spell him Intaphrenes and Intaphernes.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Gobryas
snapshots.body: One of the seven, who grappled with the Magian in the dark and told Darius to strike through both of them rather than let go.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Megabyzos
snapshots.body: One of the seven, who argued for oligarchy: nothing is more foolish or more insolent, he said, than a useless crowd.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aspathines
snapshots.body: One of the seven, who brought in Hydarnes.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hydarnes
snapshots.body: One of the seven, brought in by Aspathines.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Oibares
snapshots.body: Darius’s groom, who won him the kingdom before sunrise with a mare, a hand and a horse that neighed first.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Parmys
snapshots.body: Smerdis’s daughter, one of the wives Darius took to fasten the succession to Cyrus’s line.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Artystone
snapshots.body: Cyrus’s other daughter, a virgin, whom Darius married with Atossa.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Zopyros
snapshots.body: Megabyzos’s son, to whom a mule foaled; he cut off his own nose and ears, had himself whipped, deserted to Babylon as a mutilated man with a grievance, was given the city’s army, and handed the walls to Darius. Darius said he would rather have one Zopyros unmutilated than twenty Babylons.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Demokedes
snapshots.body: The physician of Croton, sold into Persia as Polycrates’s slave, who cured Darius’s ankle and Atossa’s breast, got everything he asked for except his freedom, and talked his way home by way of a reconnaissance of Greece. The two editions spell him Demokedes and Democedes.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Calliphon
snapshots.body: Demokedes’s father, at Croton.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Milon
snapshots.body: The wrestler of Croton, whose daughter Demokedes bought himself a betrothal to, in name, because Darius had heard of him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aristophilides
snapshots.body: King of the Tarentines, who unshipped the Persian ships’ steering-oars and locked up the crews so that Demokedes could get away to Croton.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Gillos
snapshots.body: The Tarentine exile who rescued the stranded Persians and brought them back to the king, and asked in payment only to be restored — which the Cnidians could not manage.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Tarentines
snapshots.body: Aristophilides’s people, in Italy.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Indians
snapshots.body: The most numerous nation Herodotus knows, whose Callatians eat their dead and who pay their tribute in gold dust.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The tribute nations
snapshots.body: Darius’s twenty provinces, named in a roll of some forty peoples — Chorasmians, Sogdians, Bactrians, Caspians, Parthians, Sarangians, Paricanians and the rest — each with its assessment in talents. The list is Herodotus’s proof of what the empire actually was: not a conquest story but an accounts book.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Targitaos
snapshots.body: The first man in the Scythian account of themselves, born of Zeus and a daughter of the Borysthenes; his three sons divided the kingdom by which of them could pick up the golden plough, yoke, axe and cup without being burnt.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Lipoxaïs
snapshots.body: The eldest of Targitaos’s three sons, from whom the Auchatai are descended.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Arpoxaïs
snapshots.body: The middle son, from whom the Catiaroi and Traspians come.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Colaxaïs
snapshots.body: The youngest, who alone could take up the burning gold, and from whom the Royal tribe descends.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Agathyrsos
snapshots.body: One of the three sons Heracles begot on the snake-woman in Hylaia, in the Pontic Greeks’ version of the Scythian origin.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Gelonos
snapshots.body: The second of those three sons.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Skythes
snapshots.body: The youngest of the three, the only one who could draw the bow and put on the belt, and the ancestor of all the Scythian kings.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aristeas
snapshots.body: The poet of Proconnesos who wrote the Arimaspeia, died in a fuller’s shop, was seen the same day on the road to Kyzicos, and turned up again two hundred and forty years later at Metapontion telling them to set up an altar to Apollo.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Caÿstrobios
snapshots.body: Aristeas’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Anacharsis
snapshots.body: The one Scythian the Greeks admire, killed by his own king for keeping a Greek festival — Herodotus’s single exception, with Skyles, to the rule that Scythians want nothing Greek.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Saulios
snapshots.body: King of the Scythians, who shot his brother Anacharsis with an arrow for celebrating the rites of the Mother of the Gods.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Skyles
snapshots.body: A Scythian king by a Greek mother, who kept a house at Borysthenes and was initiated into the rites of Bacchus; his own people made his brother king instead and cut off his head.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ariapeithes
snapshots.body: Skyles’s father, a Scythian king with a Greek wife from Istria.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Tymnes
snapshots.body: Ariapeithes’s steward, and one of Herodotus’s named sources for Scythian genealogy.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Idanthyrsos
snapshots.body: King of the Scythians in Darius’s invasion, who would not fight, sent back a mouse, a frog, a bird and five arrows, and told Darius to weep when he found the tombs of his fathers.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Octamasades
snapshots.body: Skyles’s brother, made king in his place, who cut off Skyles’s head — and who traded a hostage uncle with Sitalkes rather than fight him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Sitalkes
snapshots.body: The Thracian king who offered Octamasades his own brother in exchange for the one Octamasades held, so that neither had to give battle.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Salmoxis
snapshots.body: The divinity of the Getai, whom some of them call Gebeleizis, and whom the Greeks say was a man — a freed slave of Pythagoras who built an underground chamber, disappeared into it for three years, and came back to prove immortality.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pythagoras
snapshots.body: Son of Mnesarchos, named as the master whose slave Salmoxis is supposed to have been — a story Herodotus reports and does not believe.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mnesarchos
snapshots.body: Pythagoras’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mandrocles
snapshots.body: The Samian who built the bridge of boats across the Bosphorus, was richly rewarded, and spent the money on a painting of the crossing dedicated in the temple of Hera.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Sataspes
snapshots.body: The Achaemenid sent to sail round Libya instead of being impaled, who turned back in fear and was impaled after all; his eunuch ran off to Samos with a great sum.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Teaspis
snapshots.body: Sataspes’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Megabazos
snapshots.body: The Persian Darius left to command in Europe — the man whose praise Darius rated above a pomegranate’s seeds; he subdued the Hellespont and told the Persians the Chalcedonians must have been blind.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Histiaeus
snapshots.body: Tyrant of Miletus, who talked the Ionians out of breaking Darius’s bridge over the Ister on the argument that their own tyrannies depended on him. The two editions spell him Histiaeus and Histiaios.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Histiaeus
snapshots.body: Driven out of Miletus by the Milesians, he turned pirate on the Hellespont, subdued Chios and was beaten at Malene by Harpagus. He expected Darius to forgive him; Artaphrenes and Harpagus killed him at Sardis first and sent only his head, which Darius had washed and buried with honour, blaming the men who had not brought him up alive.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: The Amazons
snapshots.body: Whom the Scythians call Oiorpata, man-slayers; the ones taken at the Thermodon killed their crews, drifted to the Maeotian lake, and became the Sauromatai by marrying Scythian youths on terms.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Theras
snapshots.body: The Spartan regent who would not be a subject when his nephews came of age, and led the colony to Callista, which took his name — Thera.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Autesion
snapshots.body: Theras’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Tisamenus
snapshots.body: Autesion’s father, in the descent from Cadmus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Membliarus
snapshots.body: The Phoenician left on Callista by Cadmus, whose descendants Theras found there eight generations later.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Poikiles
snapshots.body: Membliarus’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Minyae
snapshots.body: The children of the Argonauts, driven from Lemnos, who camped on Taÿgetus, were taken in by Sparta, plotted, and were saved by their Spartan wives smuggling them out in their own clothes.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Grinnus
snapshots.body: King of Thera, who went to Delphi about something else and was told to found a city in Libya, and answered that he was too old — pointing at Battus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aesanius
snapshots.body: Grinnus’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Etearchus
snapshots.body: King of Oaxus in Crete, who let his second wife persuade him to swear away his own daughter Phronime — and handed her to a merchant to be drowned. A different man from the Etearchus of the Ammonians in Book 2.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Phronime
snapshots.body: Etearchus’s daughter, sworn away by her father, saved at sea by the Theraean who had contracted to drown her, and the mother of Battus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Themison
snapshots.body: The Theraean merchant who took the oath to throw Phronime into the sea, kept it to the letter by lowering her over the side and pulling her straight back up, and then kept her.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Polymnestus
snapshots.body: A Theraean of good family, Phronime’s husband and Battus’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Corobius
snapshots.body: The murex-fisher of Crete who had once been blown to Platea and could pilot the Theraeans there; they left him on the island with rations and forgot him for longer than the rations lasted.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Battus
snapshots.body: The founder of Cyrene, who went to Delphi about his stammer and was told to found a city in Libya instead. He reigned forty years. The older translation spells him Battos throughout.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Battus the Fortunate
snapshots.body: The third king of Cyrene, in whose reign the oracle invited all Greeks to come and share out Libyan land.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Battus the Lame
snapshots.body: Arcesilaus’s son, lame and unsound in his feet, in whose reign Cyrene sent to Delphi for a constitution and got Demonax of Mantineia. Pheretime was his wife.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Arcesilaus
snapshots.body: Battus the founder’s son, who reigned sixteen years.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Arcesilaus
snapshots.body: Battus the Fortunate’s son, who quarrelled with his brothers until they founded Barca, lost seven thousand hoplites at Leucon, and was strangled by his own brother Haliarchus while sick.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Arcesilaus
snapshots.body: Battus the Lame’s son by Pheretime, who would not keep Demonax’s constitution, was exiled to Samos, came back on a promise of land, burnt his opponents alive in a tower, and was murdered at Barca with his father-in-law.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The house of Battus
snapshots.body: The royal line of Cyrene. The oracle told Arcesilaus that Loxias granted his family four named Battus and four named Arcesilaus, eight generations, and no more — which is exactly how many there were.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Haliarchus
snapshots.body: Arcesilaus’s brother, who strangled him while he was sick from a potion, and was himself killed by treachery by Arcesilaus’s wife.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eryxo
snapshots.body: Arcesilaus’s wife, who had Haliarchus killed for murdering her husband.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Demonax
snapshots.body: The most respected man in Mantineia, sent to Cyrene to write it a constitution; he divided the people into three tribes, left the king his estates and priesthoods, and gave everything else to the people.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pheretime
snapshots.body: Battus the Lame’s wife and Arcesilaus’s mother, who sat as a suppliant of one Persian governor after another until she got an army, took Barca, impaled the men on the wall and cut off their wives’ breasts to nail up beside them — and then died eaten by worms.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Euelthon
snapshots.body: Ruler of Salamis in Cyprus, who gave Pheretime every fine gift except the army she kept asking for, and observed that a spindle was a more suitable present for a woman.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aglomachus
snapshots.body: The private citizen whose tower Arcesilaus’s enemies took refuge in, and which Arcesilaus burnt down around them.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Alazeir
snapshots.body: Arcesilaus’s father-in-law, the ruler of Barca, killed in the marketplace along with him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aryandes
snapshots.body: The Persian governor of Egypt who gave Pheretime her army, and who was afterwards put to death by Darius for coining silver as pure as the king’s gold.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Jason
snapshots.body: Whose ship, driven to Libya by a gale, is one of the origins Herodotus gives for the lake Tritonis story.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hyperoche
snapshots.body: One of the two Hyperborean maidens who brought the sacred offerings to Delos and died there.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Laodike
snapshots.body: The other Hyperborean maiden, buried with Hyperoche on Delos.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Arge
snapshots.body: One of two earlier Hyperborean maidens who came to Delos with the gods themselves.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Opis
snapshots.body: Arge’s companion, named with her in Olen’s hymn.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Olen
snapshots.body: The Lycian who composed the Delian hymn in which the Hyperborean maidens are named.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Sauromatai
snapshots.body: Descended, the story says, from the Amazons and the Scythian youths; their women ride, shoot and hunt, and no woman marries until she has killed an enemy.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Budinoi
snapshots.body: A great and numerous nation with grey eyes and red hair, in a country wholly of forest, whose city Gelonos is built of wood.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Gelonians
snapshots.body: Greeks by descent who left the trading stations and settled among the Budinoi, speaking half Scythian and half Greek.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Neuroi
snapshots.body: Who left their country because of snakes, and who are said by their neighbours — and by themselves — to become wolves once a year.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Androphagoi
snapshots.body: The man-eaters, the most savage manners of all men, with no law and no justice and a language of their own.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Melanchlainoi
snapshots.body: The Black-cloaks, who wear black and follow Scythian customs without being Scythian.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Agathyrsians
snapshots.body: A most delicate people, great wearers of gold, who hold their women in common so that they may all be brothers.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Issedonians
snapshots.body: Beyond the Argippaioi, who eat their dead fathers at a feast and gild the skull to sacrifice at yearly; their women have equal power with the men.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Arimaspians
snapshots.body: The one-eyed men beyond the Issedonians who fight the gold-guarding griffins for it — a story Herodotus repeats from Aristeas and does not vouch for.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Hyperboreans
snapshots.body: Beyond the griffins, extending to the sea; they send the sacred offerings wrapped in wheat-straw on from nation to nation until they reach Delos.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Alazonians
snapshots.body: Above the Callipidai on the Hypanis, who sow and eat grain, onions, leeks, lentils and millet.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Callipidai
snapshots.body: Greek Scythians on the Hypanis, above the trading station of the Borysthenites.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Tauroi
snapshots.body: Who sacrifice shipwrecked men and any Greek they catch to the Maiden, and nail the heads up over their houses.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Getai
snapshots.body: The bravest and most law-abiding of the Thracians, who believe they do not die but go to Salmoxis, and who shoot arrows at the sky when it thunders.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Garamantes
snapshots.body: Who flee from every man, own no weapon of war, and hunt the Cave-dwelling Ethiopians in four-horse chariots.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Lotus-eaters
snapshots.body: Who live entirely on the fruit of the lotus, about the size of a mastich-berry and as sweet as a date, and make wine of it.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Machlyes
snapshots.body: Who use the lotus too, though less, and who live round Lake Tritonis and hold the yearly festival of Athene where the maidens fight.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Auseans
snapshots.body: Neighbours of the Machlyes, who have no marriage but couple like cattle, and bring up a child in whichever house the man it resembles lives in.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Atlanteans
snapshots.body: Named after their mountain, who are said to eat nothing that has life and never to dream.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Gindanes
snapshots.body: Whose women wear an anklet of hide for every man they have lain with, and the one with the most is thought best.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Asbystae
snapshots.body: Above Cyrene, the greatest drivers of four-horse chariots in Libya.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Auschisae
snapshots.body: Above Barca, reaching down to the sea at Euesperides.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Giligamae
snapshots.body: Westward from the Adyrmachidae as far as the island of Aphrodisias, where the silphium begins.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Adyrmachidae
snapshots.body: The Libyans nearest Egypt, who follow Egyptian customs but dress like the rest, and whose brides are shown first to the king.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Cyrenaeans
snapshots.body: Battus’s colony and the richest Greek city in Libya, who invited the whole of Greece to come and take a share of land.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Theraeans
snapshots.body: Theras’s colonists on Callista, who sent Battus to Libya because the oracle would not let them alone, and whose own account of him differs from the Cyrenaean one.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Barcaeans
snapshots.body: The Cyrenaean breakaways who founded Barca, killed Arcesilaus, and were besieged nine months by the Persians and tricked out of the city by a covered pit and an oath sworn over it.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Delians
snapshots.body: Who tell more than anyone about the Hyperborean offerings and the graves of the maidens.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Borysthenites
snapshots.body: The Greeks of the trading station at the Borysthenes, who call themselves Milesians and among whom Skyles kept a house.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Royal Scythians
snapshots.body: The bravest and most numerous Scythians, who hold the rest for slaves, and whose kings are buried at Gerros with a strangled concubine, a cup-bearer, a cook and a horse.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Saspeirians
snapshots.body: Above the Medes, in Herodotus’s reckoning of the four nations that fill Asia northward.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Hellespontians
snapshots.body: Named with the Ionians and Aeolians in the fleet Darius took up the Ister.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Alexander
snapshots.body: Amyntas’s son, who had the seven Persian envoys killed at his father’s table by beardless men dressed as women, bought off the search with money and his own sister, and afterwards proved himself a Hellene at Olympia. A different man from the Alexander who carried off Helen.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Amyntas
snapshots.body: King of Macedonia, who gave Darius earth and water and let the envoys insult his women rather than risk the Persians.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Bubares
snapshots.body: The Persian to whom Alexander gave his sister Gygaea, and a great deal of money, to stop the inquiry into the missing envoys.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Gygaea
snapshots.body: Alexander’s sister, married to Bubares as part of the price of silence.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pigres
snapshots.body: One of two Paeonian brothers who set out to make themselves despots of Paeonia and showed Darius a woman carrying water, spinning and leading a horse at once — which cost their whole nation its home.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mantyes
snapshots.body: Pigres’s brother, in the same scheme.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Artaphrenes
snapshots.body: Darius’s brother, governor of Sardis, who heard Aristagoras out about Naxos and sent five hundred ships. The two editions spell him Artaphrenes and Artaphernes.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Otanes
snapshots.body: Son of Sisamnes, made commander on the coast after Megabazus and given the seat his father was flayed for — he took Byzantion, Chalcedon, Antandros and Lamponion. Not the Otanes of the seven.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Sisamnes
snapshots.body: A royal judge who took a bribe; Cambyses cut his throat, flayed him, and had the seat of judgement covered with his skin, then appointed his son to sit in it.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aristagoras
snapshots.body: Son of Molpagoras, deputy tyrant of Miletus, who talked Artaphrenes into the Naxos expedition, lost it, started the Ionian revolt to save himself, was refused by Sparta and promised twenty ships by Athens, and ran away twice — the second time to his death among the Thracians. Herodotus does not admire him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Molpagoras
snapshots.body: Aristagoras’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aristagoras
snapshots.body: Son of Heracleides, tyrant of Cyme, deposed with the rest — named once, in the same sentence as the Milesian.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Heracleides
snapshots.body: Aristagoras of Cyme’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aristagoras
snapshots.body: Tyrant of Cyzicus, one of the Hellespontine despots in Darius’s fleet at the Ister — named once, in the roll of tyrants, and not the Milesian.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Coës
snapshots.body: The Mytilenian who advised Darius to leave the bridge over the Ister standing, was given Mytilene for it, and was stoned to death by the Mytilenians when Aristagoras deposed him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Erxander
snapshots.body: Coës’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Megabates
snapshots.body: The Achaemenid cousin of Darius who commanded the Naxos fleet, quarrelled with Aristagoras over a Myndian captain tied head-out through a hawse-hole, and warned the Naxians himself.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Skylax
snapshots.body: The Myndian captain whom Megabates had bound and pushed through a hole in his own ship, and Aristagoras untied.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cleomenes
snapshots.body: King of Sparta, son of Anaxandrides by the second wife, who sent Aristagoras out of the city for saying the sea was three months from the Persian king, expelled Cleisthenes from Athens, was besieged on the Acropolis, and lost his army at Eleusis when the Corinthians went home.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cleomenes
snapshots.body: He engineered the deposing of Demaratus, sacked the grove at Argos and scourged the priest of Hera, and then went mad — striking every Spartan he met in the face with his staff. Bound in the stocks, he frightened a Helot into handing him a knife and cut himself to pieces from the legs upwards.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Dorieus
snapshots.body: Anaxandrides’s second son, who would not be ruled by his brother, failed to found a colony in Libya, tried again at Heraclea in Sicily against the oracle’s advice, and was killed there.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Leonidas
snapshots.body: Anaxandrides’s third son, named here only in the list of brothers — the man of Thermopylae.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cleombrotus
snapshots.body: Anaxandrides’s youngest son, named with Leonidas; Pausanias was his son.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Telys
snapshots.body: King of the Sybarites, against whom Dorieus is said to have helped Croton — the claim Herodotus reports and then queries.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Callias
snapshots.body: The diviner of Elis, of the Iamidae, who read the sacrifices for Croton against Sybaris and was given land for it — Herodotus’s evidence that the Crotoniats are telling the truth.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hippias
snapshots.body: Peisistratus’s son and tyrant of Athens, driven out by the Lacedaemonians and the Alcmaeonidae to Sigeum; the one man, Herodotus says, who understood the oracles about Attica.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hippias
snapshots.body: He guided the Persians in to Marathon, after a dream of lying with his own mother that he read as a return to Athens and death an old man in his own land. Then a fit of coughing loosened a tooth into the sand; he could not find it, and said that the land was not theirs after all.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Hipparchus
snapshots.body: Peisistratus’s other son, killed by Aristogeiton and Harmodius after a dream that warned him plainly and that he took no notice of.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aristogeiton
snapshots.body: With Harmodius, the killer of Hipparchus; both were Gephyraeans by descent.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Harmodius
snapshots.body: Aristogeiton’s companion in the killing.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Gephyraeans
snapshots.body: The family Aristogeiton and Harmodius came from, driven out of Tanagra by the Boeotians and received at Athens on conditions, with rites of their own that other Athenians may not attend.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Anchimolius
snapshots.body: The Spartan of repute sent by sea against the Peisistratidae, beaten by the Thessalian horse at Phalerum and buried at Alopekai.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aster
snapshots.body: Anchimolius’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Alcmaeonidae
snapshots.body: The Athenian family in exile who, Herodotus says, bribed the Pythian priestess to tell every Spartan who came that Athens must be set free — and so brought down the tyranny.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Alcmaeonidae
snapshots.body: Herodotus will not accept the charge that they signalled to the Persians with a shield after Marathon: they were in exile the whole time of the tyranny, and it was by their contrivance that the sons of Peisistratus gave up their rule. That a shield was shown he does not deny. Who showed it, he says, he cannot say.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Cleisthenes
snapshots.body: The Alcmaeonid who beat Isagoras by taking the people into his party, made ten tribes out of four, and was expelled by Cleomenes as one of the accursed — and sent for again.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cleisthenes
snapshots.body: Tyrant of Sicyon and the Athenian Cleisthenes’s mother’s father, who renamed the Dorian tribes after a pig, an ass and a swine and called his own the Rulers, and tried to turn Adrastus out of his own hero-shrine by importing Melanippus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Isagoras
snapshots.body: Son of Tisander, Cleisthenes’s rival, who called in Cleomenes and was driven out with him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Tisander
snapshots.body: Isagoras’s father, of a family Herodotus cannot trace beyond its sacrifices to Carian Zeus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Adrastus
snapshots.body: Son of Talaus, the Argive hero whose shrine stood in the marketplace of Sicyon and whose worship Cleisthenes tried to starve out. A different man from the Phrygian Adrastus of Book 1.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Talaus
snapshots.body: Adrastus’s father. The older translation spells him Talaos.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Melanippus
snapshots.body: Son of Astacus, Adrastus’s bitterest enemy, whom Cleisthenes fetched from Thebes and installed in the town hall of Sicyon so that Adrastus’s festivals could be transferred to him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Astacus
snapshots.body: Melanippus’s father. The older translation spells him Astacos.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Polybus
snapshots.body: The earlier king of the land of Sicyon, whose daughter’s son Adrastus was and whose kingdom he inherited.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aeacus
snapshots.body: Whose sons the Aeginetans sent to the Thebans instead of an army — and afterwards sent the army too, which is what the Athenians never forgave.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Socles
snapshots.body: The Corinthian who talked the allies out of restoring Hippias by telling them, at length, what a tyrant had actually been like at Corinth.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aëtion
snapshots.body: Son of Echecrates, of the deme of Petra and a Lapith by descent, who married the lame Labda when no Bacchiad would, and to whom the oracle said his wife would bear a rolling stone.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Echecrates
snapshots.body: Aëtion’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Labda
snapshots.body: The lame daughter of Amphion, whom no Bacchiad would marry, and the mother of Cypselus — whom ten men came to kill and none of them could, because she handed him to them and he smiled.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Bacchiadae
snapshots.body: The oligarchy of Corinth, who married only among themselves and tried to kill the child the oracles warned them of. The older translation spells them Bacchiadai.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Onesilus
snapshots.body: Gorgus’s younger brother, who shut him out of Salamis and led the Cyprian revolt; his head was hung over the gate of Amathus and a swarm of bees filled it, which made him a hero with an annual sacrifice.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Gorgus
snapshots.body: King of Salamis in Cyprus, shut out of his own city by his brother and restored when the revolt failed.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Chersis
snapshots.body: Gorgus and Onesilus’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Siromus
snapshots.body: Chersis’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Artybius
snapshots.body: The Persian commander in Cyprus whose horse was trained to rear against a man, and which Onesilus’s Carian groom cut the legs from.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Stesenor
snapshots.body: The despot of Curium who deserted in the middle of the Cyprian battle and took the war with him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Daurises
snapshots.body: A son-in-law of Darius, who took the towns of the Hellespont and then was drawn off to Caria and killed in a night ambush at Pedasos.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hymaees
snapshots.body: Another son-in-law of Darius and a commander in the same campaign, who took Kios and the Aeolian towns and died of illness in the Troad. The two editions spell him Hymaees and Hymaies.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pixodarus
snapshots.body: The Carian who advised crossing the Maeander and fighting with the river at their backs so that the Carians could not run — advice they did not take.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Heracleides
snapshots.body: Of Mylasa, whose plan of a night ambush on the road to Pedasos destroyed Daurises and his generals.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Paeonians
snapshots.body: Whose two brothers’ scheme brought Darius’s order to move the whole nation to Asia; those round Lake Prasias, living on platforms over the water, were never taken.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Perinthians
snapshots.body: Who had once lost to the Paeonians on a paean and a single combat of man, horse and dog, and who fought Megabazus bravely and lost to numbers.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Macedonians
snapshots.body: Amyntas’s and Alexander’s people, whose royal house Herodotus is at pains to prove Hellenic.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Boeotians
snapshots.body: Who drove the Gephyraeans out of Tanagra, and who invaded Attica with the Chalcidians while Cleomenes was at Eleusis.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Chalcidians
snapshots.body: Who invaded Attica from the other side and were beaten on the same day as the Boeotians; seven hundred of them were ransomed and their fetters hung in the Acropolis.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Thebans
snapshots.body: Who gave Cleisthenes leave to take Melanippus away, and who asked the oracle how to punish Athens and were told to ask their nearest kin.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Epidaurians
snapshots.body: Who were told by Delphi to make images of Damia and Auxesia out of Athenian olive-wood, and whose Aeginetan colonists later stole them.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Sicyonians
snapshots.body: Cleisthenes’s people, in whose marketplace Adrastus’s shrine stood and whose Dorian tribes he renamed after animals.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Cyprians
snapshots.body: Who joined the Ionian revolt under Onesilus, all but Amathus, and were beaten in a year when their own contingents deserted in the field.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Curians
snapshots.body: Of Curium, said to be colonists from Argos, whose desertion turned the Cyprian battle.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Amathusians
snapshots.body: The one Cyprian city that would not join the revolt, and which hung Onesilus’s head over its gate.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Sybarites
snapshots.body: Whose city Croton took, and who claim Dorieus helped do it.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Crotoniats
snapshots.body: Who say no stranger helped them except Callias the diviner — the version Herodotus prefers, and gives his reasons for. The older translation calls them only “the men of Croton”.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Mytilenians
snapshots.body: Who stoned Coës to death as soon as Aristagoras deposed him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Thessalians
snapshots.body: Whose thousand horse beat Anchimolius at Phalerum for the Peisistratidae, and were beaten in turn.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Naxians
snapshots.body: Whose exiles brought the Persians down on Ionia, and who were warned in time by Megabates and stood a four-month siege.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Eretrians
snapshots.body: Who sent five triremes to the Ionian revolt to repay Miletus for an older debt.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Parians
snapshots.body: Who were called in to reform the constitution of Miletus and did it by finding the men who kept their own farms in good order.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hermippus
snapshots.body: The man of Atarneus whom Histiaeus used as a courier to the Persians at Sardis. He carried the letters to Artaphrenes instead, then carried them on as instructed and brought the replies back — and many Persians died of it.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Dionysius
snapshots.body: The Phocaean commander who told the Ionians at Lade that their affairs stood on a razor edge, and drilled them for seven days until they refused to obey a man with three ships. When the line broke he took three enemy ships, sailed for Sicily and lived as a pirate, plundering Carthaginians and Tyrsenians but never Hellenes.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aeaces
snapshots.body: Tyrant of Samos, Syloson’s son, deposed by Aristagoras and sent by the Persians to offer his countrymen terms. Sixty Samian ships hoisted sail and left the line at Lade; Samos alone kept its city and its temples, and the Phoenicians put him back.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Phrynichus
snapshots.body: The Athenian who staged a play called The Capture of Miletus. The audience wept, the city fined him a thousand drachmas for reminding them of their own grief, and no one was ever to perform the play again.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Prienians
snapshots.body: Twelve ships in the Ionian line at Lade, next to the Milesians.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Teians
snapshots.body: Seventeen ships in the Ionian line at Lade.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Scythes
snapshots.body: King of Zancle, away besieging a Sicel town when the Samians walked into his empty city. Hippocrates put him in fetters for losing it; he escaped to Asia, and Darius thought him the most righteous of all the men who ever came up to him out of Hellas.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pythogenes
snapshots.body: Scythes’s brother, put in fetters with him and sent off to Inyx.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Anaxilaus
snapshots.body: Tyrant of Rhegium, at odds with Zancle, who told the Samians to leave the Fair Strand alone and take the city whose men were away.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hippocrates
snapshots.body: Tyrant of Gela, who came to rescue his Zanclaean allies and sold them instead: he chained their king, took half the movable goods and the slaves and all the land, kept most of the people for himself, and handed three hundred of their leading men to the Samians to kill.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Sicels
snapshots.body: The people of the interior of Sicily, in whose land the Fair Strand lay and against whose town the men of Zancle were encamped.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Zanclaeans
snapshots.body: The Sicilian Ionians who invited settlers to the Fair Strand, lost their own city to the men they invited, and were enslaved by the ally they called in to help.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Bisaltes
snapshots.body: A man of Abydos, left in charge of Histiaeus’s affairs on the Hellespont.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Apollophanes
snapshots.body: Bisaltes’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Harpagus
snapshots.body: The Persian commanding in Mysia who beat Histiaeus at Malene when the cavalry charged, and took him alive. Not the Mede who was made to expose Cyrus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Oebares
snapshots.body: Megabazus’s son, Persian governor at Dascyleium, with whom Cyzicus came to terms before the Phoenician fleet arrived — which is why Cyzicus was not burned.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Lysagoras
snapshots.body: Histiaeus of Miletus’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Miltiades
snapshots.body: Cimon’s son, tyrant of the Chersonese, who escaped the Phoenicians by four ships and his enemies by a trial, and was then elected general. At Marathon he talked the polemarch into fighting and waited for his own day of command. Afterwards he asked for seventy ships without saying where they were going, failed at Paros, and died of a rotting thigh with a fine of fifty talents unpaid.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Miltiades
snapshots.body: Cypselus’s son, who called the Dolonkians into his doorway and so turned out to be the founder the oracle had promised them. He walled the isthmus, was ransomed from Lampsacus by a threat of Croesus, and died childless; the Chersonese sacrifices to him still, with games no man of Lampsacus may enter.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cypselus
snapshots.body: The Athenian father of the first Miltiades. Not the tyrant of Corinth of the same name.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cimon
snapshots.body: Miltiades’s father, driven out of Athens by Peisistratus, three times a winner at Olympia with the same mares — the second victory he let Peisistratus be proclaimed for, and so bought his way home. The sons of Peisistratus had him killed by night near the City Hall; his mares are buried facing him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cimon
snapshots.body: Miltiades’s son, who paid the fifty talents his father was fined, and whom Herodotus names once more as the Athenian commander at a siege on the Thracian coast.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Stesagoras
snapshots.body: Cimon’s elder son, raised in the Chersonese by his great-uncle and heir to his rule, killed in the city hall by an axe blow from a man who passed himself off as a deserter.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Stesagoras
snapshots.body: Cimon’s father, named only in the descent of the Chersonese house.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Philaeus
snapshots.body: Ajax’s son, the first of Miltiades’s family to become an Athenian.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ajax
snapshots.body: The hero from whom Miltiades’s house traced itself, by way of Aeacus and Aegina.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Dolonkians
snapshots.body: The Thracians of the Chersonese, so hard pressed by the Apsinthians that they sent their kings to Delphi, and were told to take home as founder the first man who offered them hospitality.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Apsinthians
snapshots.body: The Thracian neighbours whose war drove the Dolonkians to the oracle, and whom Miltiades shut out with a wall across the isthmus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Olorus
snapshots.body: King of the Thracians, whose daughter Miltiades married in the Chersonese.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hegesipyle
snapshots.body: Olorus’s daughter, Miltiades’s Thracian wife.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Metiochus
snapshots.body: Miltiades’s eldest son, by an earlier wife, captured in the one ship of five that did not escape. Darius did him no harm at all: a house, an estate and a Persian wife, and his children were counted as Persians.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Euagoras
snapshots.body: The Laconian whose mares also won three Olympic victories — the only ones besides Cimon’s to do it.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mardonius
snapshots.body: Gobryas’s son and Darius’s son-in-law, sent down to the coast young. He put down the Ionian tyrants and set up popular governments — which Herodotus offers as a marvel to Hellenes who will not believe Otanes argued for popular rule — then lost three hundred ships off Athos, was wounded by the Brygi, and was relieved of his command.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Artozostra
snapshots.body: Darius’s daughter, whom Mardonius had lately married.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Thasians
snapshots.body: The islanders whose mines brought in two hundred talents a year and sometimes three hundred, spent on warships and a stronger wall — which Darius ordered pulled down, with the ships sent to Abdera.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Brygi
snapshots.body: The Thracians who attacked Mardonius’s camp by night, killed many of his men and wounded him, and were made subject all the same.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Thasus
snapshots.body: The Phoenician who made the first settlement on the island, and left it his name.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Demaratus
snapshots.body: Ariston’s son and king of Sparta of the younger house, who accused Cleomenes over Aegina out of envy and was unseated for it: the charge was that Ariston, counting the months on his fingers, had denied him at birth. He made his mother tell him whose son he was, was mocked at a festival by the man who replaced him, and went to Darius.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Leotychides
snapshots.body: Demaratus’s kinsman, who had lost his bride to him and swore the charge that unseated him. He took the throne, was sentenced to be handed over to the Aeginetans for the hostages, told the Athenians the story of Glaucus instead, and ended in exile at Tegea after being caught in camp sitting on a glove stuffed with money.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Crius
snapshots.body: The Aeginetan who told Cleomenes he had no authority from Sparta and would not be taking anyone away. Cleomenes asked his name, heard that it meant Ram, and told him to bind his horns with bronze.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Polycritus
snapshots.body: Crius’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eurysthenes
snapshots.body: The twin the Spartans took for the elder, because his mother washed and fed him first. The senior royal house descends from him, and is honoured more for it.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Procles
snapshots.body: Aristodemus’s other twin, ancestor of the younger royal house. The brothers were at variance their whole lives, and so were their descendants.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aristodemus
snapshots.body: The Heraclid who, the Lacedaemonians alone say, led them into this land himself; he lived just long enough to see his twin sons and then died of sickness.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Argeia
snapshots.body: Aristodemus’s wife, who told the Lacedaemonians she could not tell her twins apart. She knew perfectly well. She wanted both of them made kings.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aristomachus
snapshots.body: Aristodemus’s father in the Heraclid line.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cleodaeus
snapshots.body: Aristomachus’s father, Hyllus’s son.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hyllus
snapshots.body: Heracles’s son, at the head of the Spartan royal descent.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Thersander
snapshots.body: Polyneices’s son, Argeia’s great-grandfather.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Polyneices
snapshots.body: Thersander’s father, at the head of Argeia’s Theban descent.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Panites
snapshots.body: The Messenian who ended the Spartans’ difficulty: watch which twin the mother washes and feeds first, and if she always keeps the same order you have your answer.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Acrisius
snapshots.body: Danae’s father. Count back from him, Herodotus says, and the rulers of the Dorians come out Egyptian.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Helots
snapshots.body: The Lacedaemonian serfs: gathered in thousands to mourn a dead king, set to pile brushwood round the grove at Argos, sent to drag the priest of Hera from his own altar. One of them was frightened into handing Cleomenes a knife.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Ephors
