snapshots.body: The Spartan magistrates sitting with Ariston when he denied his newborn son, produced years later as witnesses against Demaratus, and hearing the charge that Cleomenes had been bribed not to take Argos.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Pythians
snapshots.body: The two men each Spartan king appoints to consult the god at Delphi, who eat at the public table with the kings and share the keeping of the oracles.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Agetus
snapshots.body: Ariston’s closest friend, who agreed to an exchange of any one possession, sworn on oath, and lost his wife by it.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Alcides
snapshots.body: Agetus’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Menares
snapshots.body: Leotychides’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Agis
snapshots.body: Menares’s father, of the same royal house as Demaratus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Percalos
snapshots.body: Chilon’s daughter, betrothed to Leotychides and carried off first by Demaratus, who married her himself. That was the beginning of the feud.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Chilon
snapshots.body: Percalos’s father. Herodotus gives him a patronymic and nothing more.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Demarmenos
snapshots.body: Chilon’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cobon
snapshots.body: The most powerful man at Delphi, bought by Cleomenes to get the answer he wanted about Demaratus, and driven into exile when the business came out. The older translation spells him Cobon and Cobin in the same sentence.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aristophantus
snapshots.body: Cobon’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Perialla
snapshots.body: The prophetess of the oracle who gave the answer Cleomenes had paid for, and was removed from her office.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Astrabacus
snapshots.body: The hero of the shrine beside Ariston’s door, who Demaratus’s mother says came to her in her husband’s likeness and left his own garlands on her. The diviners agreed it was he.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Zacynthians
snapshots.body: The islanders who let the Spartans take Demaratus’s attendants and would not give up the man.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Zeuxidemus
snapshots.body: Leotychides’s son, whom some Spartans called Cyniscus. He died before his father and never was king.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Archidamus
snapshots.body: Zeuxidemus’s son, who married his grandfather’s daughter.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eurydame
snapshots.body: Leotychides’s second wife, who bore him a daughter and no son.

snapshots.name: Menios
snapshots.body: Eurydame’s brother.

snapshots.name: Diactorides
snapshots.body: Eurydame’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Lampito
snapshots.body: Leotychides’s daughter, whom he gave in marriage to Archidamus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Casambus
snapshots.body: One of the two most powerful men on Aegina, carried off with Crius and handed to the Athenians for safekeeping.

snapshots.body: Casambus’s father.

snapshots.name: Cleander
snapshots.body: A Phigalian prophet out of Arcadia, who persuaded the slaves holding Tiryns to make war on their old masters — and the war was long.

snapshots.name: Argos
snapshots.body: The hero whose grove and sanctuary stood at Argos. Cleomenes burned the grove, then asked a deserter whose it was, and understood that the oracle promising he would conquer Argos had already been kept.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Theasides
snapshots.body: A Spartan of standing who asked the Aeginetans what they thought they were doing carrying off a king their own citizens had handed over, and talked them out of it.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Leoprepes
snapshots.body: Theasides’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Glaucus
snapshots.body: The Lacedaemonian of two generations back whose honesty was a byword, and who asked Delphi whether he might keep a deposit by swearing falsely. The Pythia told him Oath has a son. He returned the money; there is not a descendant of his left in Sparta, nor a hearth reckoned as his.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Epicydes
snapshots.body: Glaucus’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Oath
snapshots.body: The power the Pythia set against Glaucus. It has a son with no name, no hands and no feet, who runs a perjurer down without feet and seizes him without hands, and destroys his house and his whole race.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Nicodromus
snapshots.body: The Aeginetan exile who agreed to hand the island to Athens, seized the Old City on the day he had named, and found the Athenian fleet a day late. He got away by ship, and raided his own island from Sunion afterwards.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cnoethus
snapshots.body: Nicodromus’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eurybates
snapshots.body: The Argive volunteer commander at Aegina, a trained pentathlete, who killed three men in single combat and was killed by the fourth.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Sophanes
snapshots.body: The Athenian of Deceleia who killed Eurybates.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Datis
snapshots.body: The Mede who commanded against Eretria and Athens. He would not anchor off Delos, sent the Delians home with three hundred talents of frankincense burned on the altar, enslaved Eretria, and carried a stolen gilded Apollo back across the sea to be returned.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Artaphrenes
snapshots.body: Darius’s nephew, the son of the governor of Sardis, joint commander with Datis at Marathon.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Xerxes
snapshots.body: Darius’s son, named in the count of three generations under which more evils came upon Hellas than in the twenty before. His name, Herodotus says, means Warrior.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Artaxerxes
snapshots.body: Xerxes’s son, the third of the three generations; his name means Great Warrior.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Carystians
snapshots.body: The islanders who would give neither hostages nor troops against their own neighbours, and gave way only after their town was besieged and their land stripped.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aeschines
snapshots.body: The leading Eretrian who told the four thousand Athenians how his city was actually divided, and begged them to go home rather than be destroyed with it. They took his advice.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Nothon
snapshots.body: Aeschines’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Euphorbus
snapshots.body: One of the two Eretrians of note who handed the city over on the seventh day of the assault.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Alcimachus
snapshots.body: Euphorbus’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Philagrus
snapshots.body: The other Eretrian who gave the city up.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cyneas
snapshots.body: Philagrus’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Plataeans
snapshots.body: Plataea in full force on the left wing at Marathon, repaying the city that had taken them in when Sparta advised it and would not do it. The Athenian herald still prays for blessings on the Athenians and the Plataeans together.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pheidippides
snapshots.body: The Athenian long-distance runner sent to Sparta, who was there the day after he left Athens — and who said that Pan met him on Mount Parthenion and asked why the Athenians paid him no attention, being well disposed to them and useful before now.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Callimachus
snapshots.body: The polemarch, of the deme of Aphidnae, whose extra vote decided that Athens would fight. Miltiades told him the choice lay with him alone; he took the right wing, as the custom was, and was killed there.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Stesilaus
snapshots.body: One of the ten generals, killed at Marathon.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Thrasylaus
snapshots.body: Stesilaus’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cynegirus
snapshots.body: The Athenian who had his hand cut off with an axe as he took hold of the stern ornament of a Persian ship, and fell.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Euphorion
snapshots.body: Cynegirus’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Sacae
snapshots.body: The troops drawn up with the Persians themselves in the centre at Marathon, where the barbarians broke the Athenian line and pursued it inland.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Epizelos
snapshots.body: The Athenian who lost the sight of his eyes in the close fighting with no wound on him and no missile near him, and stayed blind for life. He used to say a tall man in full armour, whose beard shadowed his whole shield, passed him by and killed the man next to him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Couphagoras
snapshots.body: Epizelos’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Callias
snapshots.body: The one Athenian who dared buy Peisistratus’s goods at auction when he was driven out, and devised every other hostility he could against him. He won the horse race at Olympia and was second in the chariot, and he let each of his three daughters marry the man in Athens she chose.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Phaenippus
snapshots.body: Callias’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hipponicus
snapshots.body: Callias’s son.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Megacles
snapshots.body: Alcmaeon’s father, at the head of the Alcmaeonid line.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Megacles
snapshots.body: Hippocrates’s son, a later Megacles of the same house.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hippocrates
snapshots.body: Megacles’s other son, father of the younger Megacles and the younger Agariste.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aristonymus
snapshots.body: Cleisthenes of Sicyon’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Myron
snapshots.body: Aristonymus’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Andreas
snapshots.body: Myron’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Agariste
snapshots.body: Cleisthenes of Sicyon’s daughter, for whom he called the suitors of Hellas to Sicyon and kept them a year under test. She married Megacles, and her son gave Athens its ten tribes and its democracy.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Agariste
snapshots.body: The later Agariste of the house, named after Cleisthenes’s daughter, who dreamed she had given birth to a lion and a few days later bore Pericles.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hippocleides
snapshots.body: The suitor Cleisthenes liked best, for himself and for his Corinthian connection — until he called for a table, danced Laconian figures and Attic figures on it, and then stood on his head and waved his legs. Told he had danced his marriage away, he said that Hippocleides did not care.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Smindyrides
snapshots.body: The suitor from Sybaris, who of all men on earth had reached the highest point of luxury.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hippocrates
snapshots.body: Smindyrides’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Damasus
snapshots.body: A suitor, from Siris.

snapshots.name: Amyris
snapshots.body: Damasus’s father, the man they called the Wise.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Amphimnestus
snapshots.body: A suitor, from Epidamnus on the Ionian gulf.

snapshots.name: Epistrophus
snapshots.body: Amphimnestus’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Males

snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Titormus
snapshots.body: Males’s brother, who surpassed all Hellenes in strength and went off to the remotest part of Aetolia to get away from the company of men.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Leocedes
snapshots.body: The suitor from the Peloponnese, Pheidon’s son.

snapshots.name: Pheidon
snapshots.body: Tyrant of Argos, who fixed the measures the Peloponnese still uses, and outdid every other Hellene in arrogance: he threw the Eleans out of the presidency of their own games and presided himself.

snapshots.name: Amiantus
snapshots.body: An Arcadian suitor, from Trapezus.

snapshots.name: Laphanes
snapshots.body: An Azanian suitor, from the city of Paios.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Euphorion
snapshots.body: Laphanes’s father, who the Arcadians say entertained the Dioscuri in his house and from then on made a point of taking in everyone who came.

snapshots.name: Onomastus

snapshots.name: Diactorides
snapshots.body: The Thessalian suitor, of the Scopad family of Crannon.

snapshots.name: Xanthippus

snapshots.name: Timo
snapshots.body: The Parian under-priestess of the chthonic goddesses, a prisoner, who told Miltiades what to do to take Paros. snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Thoas

snapshots.name: Ariston
snapshots.body: Tyrant of Byzantium, one of the Hellespontine despots who voted at the Ister bridge. Named once, and not the king of Sparta.
